p: וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם שְׁבַע עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה וַיְהִי יְמֵי יַעֲקֹב שְׁנֵי חַיָּיו שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים וְאַרְבָּעִים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה.
— Jacob lived in the land of Egypt for seventeen years, and the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were seven years and forty and one hundred years.
מָצִינוּ בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁהַפְּרָטִים מִשְּׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב לֹא נִכְתְּבוּ בְּפֵירוּשׁ רַק בְּרֶמֶז
— We find in the Torah that the details of Jacob’s years are not written explicitly, but only allusively,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (מְגִילָּה יז.) לָמָּה נִמְנוּ שְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל יִשְׁמָעֵאל כְּדֵי לְיַחֵס בָּהֶן שְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב
— as stated in Megillah 17a: Why were Ishmael’s years enumerated? To establish Jacob’s chronology by them.
שֶׁלְּמֵדִין שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵךְ בֶּן ס״ג וְשֶׁהָיָה י״ד שָׁנָה בְּבֵית עֵבֶר וְלֹא נִכְתַּב בְּפֵירוּשׁ
— From this we learn that he received the blessing at sixty-three and spent fourteen years in Eber’s academy, though these are not stated explicitly.
וּבִפְרָט כָּאן דִּכְתִיב שֶׁבְּבוֹאוֹ לְמִצְרַיִם אָמַר לְפַרְעֹה יְמֵי שְׁנֵי מְגוּרַי שְׁלֹשִׁים וּמְאַת שָׁנָה
— This is especially striking here: Scripture records that upon arriving in Egypt he told Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my sojournings are one hundred and thirty years.”
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁכָּתוּב שֶׁחַי קמ״ז שָׁנָה הֲרֵי נֵדַע שֶׁהָיָה בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם י״ז שָׁנָה.
— Once it states that he lived one hundred and forty-seven years, we already know that he spent seventeen years in Egypt.
וְלָמָּה מוֹנֶה שְׁנוֹתָיו בִּפְרָט וְאַחַר כָּךְ בִּכְלָל.
— Why, then, does it enumerate his years first separately and afterward as a total?

paragraphs.text: Megillah 17a:1–5: “Why were Ishmael’s years enumerated? To establish Jacob’s years by means of them. For it is written: “These are the years of Ishmael’s life: one hundred and thirty-seven years.” How much older was Ishmael than Isaac? Fourteen years, for it is written: “Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram,” and: “Abraham was one hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.” It is also written: “Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.” How old was Ishmael when Jacob was born? Seventy-four. How many of his years remained? Sixty-three. It was taught: Our father Jacob was sixty-three when his father blessed him, and Ishmael died at that time. It is written: “Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob … Esau went to Ishmael and took Mahalath, Ishmael’s daughter, the sister of Nebaioth.” Once it says “Ishmael’s daughter,” do I not know that she was Nebaioth’s sister? This teaches that Ishmael betrothed her and died, and her brother Nebaioth married her off. Sixty-three, and fourteen until Joseph was born, make seventy-seven. “Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh” makes one hundred and seven; seven years of plenty and two of famine make one hundred and sixteen. Yet it is written: “Pharaoh said to Jacob: How many are the days of the years of your life? Jacob said to Pharaoh: The days of the years of my sojournings are one hundred and thirty years.” They amount only to one hundred and sixteen! We must therefore conclude that the fourteen years he spent in the house of Eber were not included. For it was taught: Jacob was secluded in the house of Eber for fourteen years. Eber died two years after our father Jacob went down to Aram Naharaim. Jacob left there and came to Aram Naharaim; thus he was seventy-seven when he stood at the well.”

p: אָכֵן אִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (רטז ב) דְּהָא כָּל יוֹמוֹי לָא אִקְרֵי וַיְחִי בְּגִין דְּכָל יוֹמוֹי בְּצַעֲרָא הֲווֹ עֲלֵיהּ כְּתִיב לֹא שָׁלַוְתִּי וְגוֹמֵר בָּתַר דְּנָחַת לְמִצְרַיִם אִקְרֵי וַיְחִי וְכוּלֵי וְדִיְּיקוּ מִדְּלָא כְתִיב וַיֵּשֶׁב יַעֲקֹב וְגוֹמֵר וְכָתוּב וַיְחִי.

— Indeed, the holy Zohar (216b) teaches that throughout his earlier days he was not described by “he lived,” because all his days were spent in suffering; concerning him it is written, “I was not at ease,” and so forth. After he descended to Egypt, he was described by “he lived,” and so forth. They infer this from Scripture’s writing “Jacob lived” rather than “Jacob dwelt,” and so forth.
כִּי הַי״ז שָׁנָה שֶׁהָיָה בְּמִצְרַיִם הֶחֱיָה גַּם אוֹתָם הַשָּׁנִים שֶׁעָבְרוּ עָלָיו.
— For the seventeen years he spent in Egypt also brought life to the years that had previously passed over him.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ה) כָּל שֶׁהִשִּׂיגַתּוּ שָׁנָה אַחַת טוֹבָה סָמוּךְ לְזִקְנָתוֹ סִימָן יָפֶה לוֹ וְכוּלֵי וְהֶעֱלָה עָלָיו הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא כְּאִלּוּ כָּל יָמָיו הָיָה בְּטוֹבָה.

— As the Sages said (Seder Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 5), whoever experiences one good year near his old age has a favorable sign, and so forth; the Holy One, blessed be He, accounts it to him as though all his days had been good.
כִּי כָּל יְמֵי יַעֲקֹב שֶׁהָיָה בְּצַעֲרָא לֹא נִקְרְאוּ חַיִּים אֵצֶל יַעֲקֹב כִּי לֹא נִשְׁלַם בִּקְדוּשָּׁתוֹ וְרַק בְּמִצְרַיִם זָכָה לְהִשְׁתַּלֵּם בִּקְדוּשָּׁתוֹ.
— For all Jacob’s days of suffering were not called life in his case, because his holiness had not yet been perfected. Only in Egypt did he merit to attain perfection in his holiness.

וְלִכְאוֹרָה לְפִי הַשֵּׂכֶל כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל מָקוֹם הַמְקוּדָּשׁ מִכָּל הָעוֹלָם וּלְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֶךְ לְךָ וְגוֹמֵר וְשָׁם אֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל.

— Yet reason would seemingly dictate otherwise: the Land of Israel is the holiest place in the world, and the Holy One, blessed be He, told our patriarch Abraham, peace be upon him, “Go for yourself,” and so forth, and there, “I will make you a great nation.”
וּלְיִצְחָק אָמַר גּוּר בָּאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת וְגוֹמֵר וְהָאָבוֹת וְגַם יַעֲקֹב בְּעַצְמוֹ חִבְּבוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ.
— To Isaac He said, “Sojourn in this land,” and so forth; the patriarchs, including Jacob himself, cherished the land.
הָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּלֵּם יַעֲקֹב בִּקְדוּשָּׁתוֹ בָּאָרֶץ הַקְּדוֹשָׁה וְלֹא בְּמִצְרַיִם בָּאָרֶץ הַטְּמֵאָה וְעַמָּהּ מְזוֹהָמִים יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הָעוֹלָם.
— It would have been fitting for Jacob’s holiness to be perfected in the holy land, rather than in Egypt, an impure land whose people were more defiled than any others in the world.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, 216b: “Here it says, “He lived.” Throughout all his earlier days it had not been called “he lived,” because all his days had been spent in suffering. Of him it is written: “I was not at ease, I was not quiet, I had no rest, and turmoil came.” After he went down to Egypt it says, “He lived.” He saw his son a king; he saw all his sons worthy and righteous, all enjoying the world’s delights and comforts, while he sat among them like good wine resting on its lees. Then it says, “Jacob lived.” There is no separation between “they were fruitful and multiplied greatly” and “Jacob lived,” and so it should be. “Seventeen years”—why seventeen years? Rabbi Shimon said: All Jacob’s days had been spent in suffering. When he saw Joseph standing before him, whenever Jacob looked at Joseph he felt whole within himself, as though he saw Joseph’s mother, for Joseph’s beauty resembled Rachel’s beauty. He felt as though he had never experienced suffering in all his days.”

paragraphs.text: Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 5: “Immediately the mercy of the Holy One, blessed be He, was stirred, and He gave Jacob seventeen good years near his old age, resembling the World to Come. From here they said: Whoever experiences one good year near his old age has a favorable sign; whoever experiences one bad year near his old age has an unfavorable sign. Our father Jacob enjoyed goodness during the seventeen years he was in Egypt, and the Holy One, blessed be He, accounted it to him as though all his days had been good, as it says: “Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years.””

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem MiShmuel, Vayechi 6:2–3: “‘Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years.’ In the holy Zohar: ‘All his days he was not called “he lived,” because all his days were spent in suffering… After he descended to Egypt he was called “he lived.”’ This needs understanding. One could say this of lesser men, whose life is not pleasant to them because of suffering, so that their life is no life; but not of Jacob, who was wholly for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be He, whose whole life was only for the service of Hashem, and nothing of his service was lessened by the suffering. It appears that, as the Arizal teaches in Likkutei Torah, in the hundred and thirty years Jacob lived before his descent to Egypt he rectified the sin of Adam’s hundred and thirty years, which was a blemish of the covenant. One who guards the covenant is called ‘living’ in the plain sense as well, for he is full of vitality and joy, while a blemish of the covenant brings a spirit of sadness and the absence of vitality and joy. So with Jacob: although he was a man free of any dross, since the rectification of Adam’s sin of a hundred and thirty years was placed upon his shoulders, as long as the rectification was not complete that sin of Adam troubled him and kept complete vitality and joy from him. This is the Zohar’s ‘all his days he was not called “he lived”’: Jacob’s vitality, which is very great vitality and joy, came only in the land of Egypt, after the rectification was complete. … Jacob, whose essence was to be in very great vitality and joy, when it was not so in completeness, even though compared with others it would count as vitality and joy, for him it counted as a lack, and from this actual suffering was drawn upon him.”

p: אָכֵן מָצִינוּ כְּמוֹ כֵן בְּגָלוּת בָּבֶל וּבְגָלוּת בַּיִת שֵׁנִי שֶׁעִיקַּר הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הָיָה דַּיְיקָא בְּבָבֶל.
— Indeed, we find a similar phenomenon in the Babylonian exile and the exile following the Second Temple: the principal expansion of the Oral Torah took place specifically in Babylonia.
וְדַיְיקָא שָׁם נִתְגַּלָּה לָהֶם רָזֵי הַתּוֹרָה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא נִתְגַּלָּה לָהֶם בְּיִשְׁבָם עַל אַדְמָתָם וְדַיְיקָא בְּבָבֶל הָיוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה.
— Precisely there, secrets of Torah were revealed to them that had not been revealed while they dwelt on their own soil; and precisely in Babylonia were the Men of the Great Assembly.
וְאָמְרוּ (סוּכָּה מד.) דִּלְהוֹן הִיא וְכֵן (שָׁם כ.) עָלָה עֶזְרָא מִבָּבֶל וִיסְדָהּ חָזְרָה וְנִשְׁתַּכְּחָה עָלָה הִלֵּל וְכוּלֵי עָלוּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא וּבָנָיו וִיסְדוּהָ.

— The Sages said (Sukkah 44a), “It is theirs.” Likewise (ibid. 20a): Ezra came up from Babylonia and established it; it was again forgotten, and Hillel came up, and so forth; Rabbi Chiyya and his sons came up and established it.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַתַּלְמוּד בַּבְלִי שֶׁהוּא עִיקַּר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁלָּנוּ וְנִתְיַיסֵּד בְּבָבֶל.
— Afterward came the Babylonian Talmud, the principal foundation of our Oral Torah, which was established in Babylonia.
וְאָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ד ד) צַדִּיקִים הֶעֱמִידָה לִי בְּחוּרְבָּנָהּ יוֹתֵר מִצַּדִּיקִים שֶׁהֶעֱמִידָה לִי בְּבִנְיָנָהּ.
— And they said (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:4): “She produced for Me more righteous people in her destruction than she produced for Me while she was built.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla §52, par. 34: “Haman arose at the beginning of the growth of the foundation of the Oral Torah, through the Men of the Great Assembly. … It is known that for anything to be born, it must necessarily first undergo dissolution and become as nothing, just as a seed decays in the earth before it sprouts. So too, in exile, Torah was altogether forgotten among the nation as a whole, to the point that they discovered it written that they should make sukkot, for they had not known of this. Although their hearts were especially steadfast with Hashem, Torah study there was in a state of sleep and concealment. That is why it is called Elam, an expression of concealment.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Rav Tzadok explains why the Oral Torah can emerge precisely from exile: the seed’s apparent dissolution precedes a new form of growth. His distinction between a steadfast heart and a dormant life of Torah gives substance to the present teaching that concealment can hold the conditions of a greater revelation.

h: Creation in Space Time and Soul

p: וְהִנֵּה בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם הָיָה בִּי״ב מַזָּלוֹת בָּרָקִיעַ הַיְינוּ בָּעוֹלָם.
— Now the creation of the world involved twelve constellations in the firmament, corresponding to the dimension of space.
וְי״ב חֳדָשִׁים בַּשָּׁנָה הוּא בַּזְּמַן כִּי לְכָךְ נִקְרֵאת שָׁנָה שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן שֵׁנִית שֶׁהַחַמָּה חָזְרָה לִמְקוֹמָהּ הָרִאשׁוֹן וְתַקִּיף הָעוֹלָם פַּעַם שֵׁנִי.
— The twelve months of the year correspond to time: it is called shanah, related to “a second time,” because the sun returns to its original place and circles the world a second time.
וְי״ב שְׁבָטִים הוּא בַּנֶּפֶשׁ כִּי כָּל מַה שֶּׁנִּבְרָא הֵם בְּעוֹלָם שָׁנָה נֶפֶשׁ כַּיָּדוּעַ בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה.
— The twelve tribes correspond to the soul, for everything created exists in the dimensions of space, time, and soul, as is known from Sefer Yetzirah.
וְהַכֹּל נִבְרָא בְּהַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא כְּלִי אוּמָּנֻתוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב רֵישׁ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה) וְיֵשׁ בְּסֵפֶר בְּרֵאשִׁית גַּם כֵּן י״ב פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת.
— Everything was created through the Torah, His artisan’s instrument (as stated at the beginning of Bereishit Rabbah); the Book of Genesis likewise contains twelve Torah portions.
וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק יְהִי אוֹר וְכֵן בְּהַבְּאֵרוֹת דְּיִצְחָק חָשְׁבוּ כְּנֶגֶד חֲמִשָּׁה חוּמְשֵׁי תוֹרָה.
— In Bereishit Rabbah, on the verse “Let there be light,” and likewise concerning Isaac’s wells, they enumerate correspondences to the five books of the Torah.
וְאָמַר שָׁם עַל סֵפֶר בְּרֵאשִׁית שֶׁבּוֹ נִתְעַסֵּק הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וּבָרָא אֶת עוֹלָמוֹ.
— There it says concerning the Book of Genesis that the Holy One, blessed be He, occupied Himself with it and created His world.
הַיְינוּ שֶׁכָּל סֵפֶר זֶה וְסִיפּוּרָיו הוּא כְּלַל בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁנִּשְׁלַם בִּקְבוּרַת יוֹסֵף שֶׁהוּא הַצַּדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם.
— That is, this entire book and its narratives encompass the creation of the world, completed with the burial of Joseph, the righteous one who is the foundation of the world.
וּכְלַל פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ בְּסִיפּוּר חַיּוּת יַעֲקֹב וּפְטִירָתוֹ וּבִרְכַּת הַשְּׁבָטִים.
— This Torah portion as a whole recounts Jacob’s life, his passing, and the blessing of the tribes.

These are the twelve governing organs in the soul: two hands, two feet, two kidneys, the spleen, liver, gallbladder, omasum, stomach, and gizzard.”

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 1:1: “Another interpretation: Amon means ‘craftsman.’ The Torah says: I was the instrument of the Holy One’s craftsmanship. Ordinarily, when a human king builds a palace, he does not build it according to his own understanding, but according to an architect’s understanding. The architect, too, does not proceed solely from his own understanding: he has plans and notebooks showing how to make rooms and doorways. So the Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world. The Torah says, ‘In the beginning God created.’ ‘Beginning’ means Torah, as it says, ‘The Lord acquired me at the beginning of His way.’”

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 3:5: “Rabbi Simon said: Light is mentioned here five times, corresponding to the five books of the Torah. ‘God said, Let there be light’ corresponds to Genesis, with which the Holy One, blessed be He, occupied Himself in creating His world. ‘And there was light’ corresponds to Exodus, in which Israel emerged from darkness into light. ‘God saw that the light was good’ corresponds to Leviticus, which is filled with many laws. ‘God separated the light from the darkness’ corresponds to Numbers, which distinguishes those who left Egypt from those who entered the Land. ‘God called the light day’ corresponds to Deuteronomy, which is filled with many laws. The companions objected to Rabbi Simon: ‘But Leviticus is already filled with many laws!’ He replied: ‘Deuteronomy repeats a matter as well.’”

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 64:8: ““Isaac again dug.” How many wells did our father Isaac dig in Beersheba? Rabbi Yehudah said: Four, corresponding to the four divisions into which his children were arranged in the wilderness. The Rabbis said: Five, corresponding to the five books of the Torah. “He called the well Esek” corresponds to Genesis, in which the Holy One, blessed be He, occupied Himself with creating the world. “He called it Sitnah” corresponds to Exodus, because “they embittered their lives with hard labor.” “They found there a well of living water” corresponds to Leviticus, which is filled with many laws. “He called it Shivah” corresponds to Numbers, which completes seven books of Torah. Are there not only five? Bar Kappara divided Numbers into three books: from its opening until “When the Ark traveled” is one book; “When the Ark traveled” and the following verse are a separate book; and from the end of that passage until the end of Numbers is a separate book. “He called it Rechovot” corresponds to Deuteronomy, because “when Hashem enlarges,” and “now Hashem has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.””

h: The Mystery of the Closed Portion

p: וּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ סְתוּמָה וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה נָתְנוּ טְעָמִים מִפְּנֵי מָה פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ סְתוּמָה וְכוּלָּם דִּבְרֵי אֱמֶת.
— This portion is closed, without the customary preceding space. Our Sages, of blessed memory, gave reasons why it is closed, and all their explanations are true.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן טַעַם לִסְתִימָתָהּ כִּי בֶאֱמֶת הָעִנְיָן הַזֶּה שֶׁיּוּשְׁלַם יַעֲקֹב בִּקְדוּשָּׁתוֹ דַּיְיקָא בְּמִצְרַיִם וְלֹא בָּאָרֶץ.
— We may offer another reason for its being closed: this very matter—that Jacob’s holiness should be perfected specifically in Egypt and not in the land—
וְשֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה וְיַגִּיעַ לָעוֹלָם כְּלַל הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל נְפָשׁוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת מוּכָנִים לְקַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה דַּיְיקָא בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ וְלֹא בָּאָרֶץ.
— and that the collective Congregation of Israel, holy souls prepared to receive the Torah, should be revealed and come into the world specifically outside the land rather than within it—
וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה גְּמַר הַבְּרִיאָה גַּם כֵּן בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה.
— and that creation’s completion should likewise occur in this place—
הֵם עִנְיָנִים סְתוּמִים וְנֶעֱלָמִים מִשֵּׂכֶל הָאָדָם לַהֲבִינָם.
— these are matters closed and concealed from human reason’s capacity to understand.
וְאָמְרוּ (רֵישׁ תּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים) מֶה הָיוּ הַפְסָקוֹת מְשַׁמְּשׁוֹת לִיתֵּן רֶיוַח לְמֹשֶׁה לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן בֵּין פָּרָשָׁה לְפָרָשָׁה.
— The Sages said (at the beginning of Torat Kohanim): What purpose did the breaks serve? To give Moses space to reflect between one section and the next.
וּמֵאֲשֶׁר הָעִנְיָן הַזֶּה עָמוֹק מְאֹד שֶׁאֵין בְּשֵׂכֶל הָאָדָם לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן לָזֹאת הִיא סְתוּמָה.
— Since this matter is so profound that human reason cannot fathom it, this portion is closed.

Once our father Jacob died, Israel’s enslavement in Egypt began. Another interpretation: Why is it closed? Because our father Jacob wished to reveal the end of the exile, but it was concealed from him. Another interpretation: Why is it closed? Because God closed off from him all the troubles of the world.”

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים מְרַמֵּז לָנוּ בָּעִנְיָן הַזֶּה שֶׁלֹּא יִמַּס לְבָבֵנוּ מֵאֲשֶׁר אֲנַחְנוּ בְּעִקְבְתָא דִמְשִׁיחָא וּבְכָל דּוֹר הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִתְקַטְּנִים וְאֵיךְ נִזְכֶּה לְהַגְּאוּלָּה.
— In any event, this teaches us not to lose heart because we live in the footsteps of the Messiah, while souls diminish in each generation, prompting the question of how we can merit redemption.
כִּי רוֹאִים אֲנַחְנוּ מַה שֶּׁקָּרָה לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ בְּגָלוּתָם וְדַיְיקָא בְּגָלוּת הִגִּיעוּ לְכָל הַקְּדוּשּׁוֹת כִּי כֵן רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
— For we see what happened to our ancestors in their exile: precisely in exile they attained all these forms of holiness, because such is Hashem’s will.
וְשָׁמַעְתִּי בְּשֵׁם הָרַב הַקָּדוֹשׁ מִפְּרְשִׁיסְחָא זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה שֶׁאַף שֶׁהַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִתְקַטְּנִים בְּכָל דּוֹר.
— I heard in the name of the holy Rabbi of Przysucha, of righteous memory, that although souls diminish in every generation,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַנְּקוּדָּה שֶׁבַּלֵּב נִטְהָר בְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר יוֹתֵר:
— nevertheless, the point within the heart becomes purer with every successive generation.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Baal HaSulam, Introduction to the Zohar §63: “Therefore, in our generation, although these souls are the lowest in their essential quality—for this reason they could not be refined into holiness until today—nevertheless, they complete the spiritual configuration of the world and of the totality of souls in respect of the vessels. The work can be completed only through them. For now the vessels of Netzach, Hod, and Yesod are being completed, and the configuration possesses all its vessels: head, middle, and end. Complete levels of light are therefore drawn into the head, middle, and end, for all who are worthy of them: complete Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, as explained above. Thus only with the completion of these lower souls can the higher lights be revealed, and not before.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: This later Kabbalistic comparison offers a complementary answer to Rav Tzadok’s question about redemption in generations of diminished souls: the stature of individual souls and the completion of the collective work are different measures. Later souls can supply what is still missing from the whole; this is a comparison with Rav Tzadok, not a claim of historical influence.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vaetchanan 21:1: “‘A future’ means that the good is seen openly, as was said of Ruth (Bava Batra 14b), ‘a calamity that has a future,’ for they saw that David came from it; and so, at once in the Babylonian exile, they saw that the Oral Torah spread through the Men of the Great Assembly. … And this is ‘a future and a hope’: the hope is for what is yet to come, as I heard from our holy master, of blessed memory, who said in the name of Rabbi Bunim, of blessed memory, that although the minds of the generations diminish each time, the point of life in the heart continually widens and becomes more refined each time in exile. Our holy master said that this was a new thing to him when he heard it in Przysucha, and afterward he found the matter stated explicitly in several places, but he did not explain to us where. We have already given a root for this, and it is explained elsewhere. And this is the good hope in exile.”

h: The 17 years that Jacob was in Egypt revived some of those bad years which befell him. This idea is stated (in ) that if an individual lives a good year close to his old age, it is a good sign for him, and G-d considers it as if all his days were good. All the days of Jacob when he was in pain was not considered to be life because they were not completed in holiness (?) and only in Egypt did he merit to complete them in his holiness. Logic would dictate that since Israel is the place of greatest holiness in the world, as G-d told Abraham to leave Aram and go to the land of Israel, and Isaac was told that he would be blessed if he lived in this land. Jacob himself loved the land, and it would have been fitting for Jacob to complete his life in holiness in the holy land, and not in Egypt which is an impure land, and its people are more polluted than any other.

We find that in the exile in Babylon and in the exile of the second Temple that the main expansion of the oral Torah was specifically in exile. Specifically there the secrets of the Torah were revealed, more than was revealed while the Jews were in Israel. It is specifically from Babylon that the people of the great assembly arose and they were able to establish the law of Arava (c.f. Sukkah 44a) We also see in Sukkah (20A) that Ezra rose from Babylon and established Torah, and thereafter Torah was forgotten. Hillel then went and re-established it (and Hillel was also from Babylon (ed)), Rabbi Chiya and his sons (from Babylon) reconstituted the Torah. It also states in Medrash Shir Hashirim (4:4) that the righteous after the destruction of the Temple constituted the Torah in a greater way than the righteous in their building of the Temple.

Behold, the creation of the world was with the 12 signs of the zodiac and relates to the creation of the world in space. The 12 months form the year (SHANA) which is called a SHANA because the sun returns to its original place in the sky a second time (SHEINIS) and strengthens the world a second time. The world in time has 12 elements. The 12 tribes represent the soul, because they are the elements which create time and space as is mentioned in SEFER HAYETZIRA. Everything was created with the Torah, which is G-d's tools (as is expressed in Bereishis Rabbah) and in the book of Bereishit there are 12 Parshiot... The medrash says further that G-d looked into the book of Bereishis and created the world. this means that this whole book and its stories are part of the creation of the world which was completed with the burial of Yosef who is the righteous one - the pillar of the world. It is also connected to the story of the last years of Yaakov, his death as well as the blessings given to the tribes of Israel.

This Parasha is closed. Our Rabbis have explained the reasons for it, and they are all true. There is another reason for it being closed. The completion of Jacob's holiness is specifically in Egypt, and not in the land of Israel. This coincides with the notion that the revelation and arrival of the Jewish People which contains the souls which were prepared for the acceptance of the Torah specifically in a foreign land and not in Israel, and that the end of the creation of the world occurs in the land of Egypt. These concepts are closed(Satum) from human understanding.

They have said (in the beginning of Vayikra Rabbah) that the purpose of the spaces in the Torah are there in order to give Moshe pause for thought between each parashah. When something is beyond the understanding of man it is closed.

Nonetheless, this whole parasha alludes to the fact that we should not become discouraged as we are in the in the birth pangs leading to the Messiah, and in every generation the souls become smaller, and how is it possible for us to achieve the final redemption? The answer lies in the fact that we see what happened to the Jewish people specifically when they were in exile, and specifically in exile they arrived to the exalted levels of holiness because this is the will of G-d. I also heard in the name of the Rebbe from Parshische of blessed memory, that even though the souls of each generation decrease. nonetheless the hole/point in our hearts becomes more holy in every generation.
